title: Evidence and decision mechanisms
goals: Distinguish an observed result from an explanation of how it was produced
Identify written rules, learned models and human decisions inside one product
Explain what additional evidence is needed when a mechanism is unknown

prerequisite.prompt: A classroom clock speaks the time. Write one thing you observed and one thing you cannot determine just from hearing it.
prerequisite.answer: You observed spoken time. Speech alone does not tell you whether the message was selected by a timetable, a learned system or a person.

vocabulary: The process that produces a result
An instruction specified by a person before the system applies it
A system whose adjustable values were fitted using examples
Information that supports or challenges a particular claim
A product that combines more than one kind of process

lesson.title: One display can hide several decisions

blocks.text: The school bus display says DELAY 12 MINUTES in red. Leila calls it AI because it predicted the delay. Arun calls it a simple rule because the number turned red. Both have noticed a real part of the product, but neither has explained the whole system. To investigate, ask which decision you are talking about and what evidence reveals how that decision was made.

An output is what a system produces. A mechanism is how it produces that output. Seeing a red number establishes its colour; it does not reveal where the number came from. Similar outputs can come from different mechanisms, and one product can contain several mechanisms.

For this lesson we have an engineering note: the delay estimator was fitted using records of earlier bus journeys; a person wrote the colour instruction; and the driver can replace the message. These are supplied facts for our classroom case. In a real investigation, we would need trustworthy documentation, a demonstration of the process or another source of mechanism evidence.

blocks.title: The bus display contains three mechanisms
rows: Delay model fitted on earlier journeys
Written rule red when delay is greater than 10
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right. The first row predicts a number, the second chooses a colour, and the third shows a human override. A correct colour does not establish that the delay prediction is correct.

blocks.text: In the first row, fitting means adjusting a model using examples. Applying the fitted model to a new journey is a different step. The model can produce an incorrect estimate even if it was trained carefully. In the second row, a written threshold compares the estimate with 10. It can follow its instructions perfectly while using a bad estimate. In the third row, a person makes the message decision.

AI is a broader field than learning from examples. It also includes approaches that represent knowledge and reason with rules. Therefore, do not use the shortcut that every rule is non-AI. In this case, a simple colour switch is ordinary automation; identifying that switch does not classify every other part of the bus system.

Question: Does the red display prove that a learned model was used? First separate the claim from the observation. The observation is that the displayed number is red. The claim concerns the process that produced the number. Next find relevant evidence. The engineering note says earlier journeys were used to fit the delay estimator. That note supports a learned-model classification for the estimator. The red colour alone does not.

rows: The estimator uses a learned model
The note describes fitting on past journeys
Only the displayed colour is observed
The driver override is a model prediction
A driver selects the replacement message

blocks.text: A strong answer states its limit: I can identify these three mechanisms from the supplied note, but I cannot infer the model's accuracy from one estimate. Even if the bus arrives exactly 12 minutes late, one success does not establish that the estimator will always work.

lesson.title: Finish an explanation with less help

blocks.text: A photo library predicts whether a picture contains a bicycle using a model fitted to labelled pictures. A written rule places all bicycle predictions in one album. The owner can move any photo to a different album. Complete the explanation in your workbook: the prediction stage is ___ because ___; the automatic album step is ___ because ___; the manual move is ___.

If a photograph lands in the wrong album, do not immediately blame the written album rule. The prediction might have been wrong, the album rule might have been implemented incorrectly, or a person might have moved the photo. Inspect the intermediate prediction and the action record to distinguish these causes.

blocks.label: Complete the three classifications and name one record that would help diagnose a misplaced photo

lesson.title: Use a question that could change your mind

blocks.text: A robot vacuum is advertised as smart. The advertisement tells you almost nothing about its decisions. A useful question is not Does it look intelligent? Ask instead how it selects a route, whether adjustable values were fitted using examples, or when a person supplies a command. It may combine several answers.

Sometimes the honest conclusion is that the mechanism is unknown. That is a precise answer when you identify the missing evidence. It is weaker to guess a mechanism and then treat your guess as a fact. Keep observations, supplied evidence and assumptions separate in your investigation.

blocks.label: A device speaks a correct answer. Explain why neither speech nor correctness alone identifies its mechanism

workbook.title: Separate observations from explanations
workbook.prompt: A door opens when a visitor approaches. Its label says intelligent entrance. List two observations and write one mechanism question whose answer would help classify the opening decision.
workbook.answer: Observations include that the door opened when the visitor approached and that its label says intelligent entrance. A useful question asks whether a written sensor threshold, a model fitted on examples or a person controls opening. The label is an observed marketing claim, not mechanism evidence.

workbook.title: Complete the photo library explanation
workbook.prompt: Use the photo-library case from the lesson. Classify the prediction, album-placement rule and owner move. A bicycle photo is in the wrong album. Name the first two records you would inspect.
workbook.answer: Prediction is learned because it was fitted using labelled pictures. Album placement is a written rule; the owner move is human control. Inspect the stored prediction and the placement or move record. A wrong album alone cannot distinguish prediction error from a later action.

workbook.title: Challenge an unsupported conclusion
workbook.prompt: Maya says a vacuum must learn because it changes direction after hitting a chair. Give two different mechanisms consistent with that observation. What evidence would distinguish them?
workbook.answer: A written contact-sensor rule could turn the vacuum, or a learned navigation model could choose a turn. A person could also control it. Documentation of the route-selection process or a controlled trace could distinguish these mechanisms. Direction change alone is insufficient.

workbook.title: Investigate a new hybrid system
workbook.prompt: A school greenhouse estimates tomorrow's temperature using a model fitted on historical weather. A written rule displays CHECK PLANTS above 30 degrees C. A caretaker chooses whether to open a vent. Identify each mechanism and explain why a correct CHECK PLANTS message would not prove an accurate temperature prediction.
workbook.answer: The forecast is learned-model prediction; the message is a written threshold; vent opening is the caretaker's decision. The message may correctly follow a forecast that is itself inaccurate. Compare the forecast with a predefined temperature observation at the relevant place and time before judging prediction accuracy.

workbook.title: Design an evidence card
workbook.prompt: Invent one product containing two mechanisms. State the supplied facts, draw an information path and write one claim the facts support and one they do not. Do not use real classmates' personal information.
workbook.answer: Accept a coherent case such as a trained speech recogniser supplying text to a written keyword rule. The support must connect to supplied facts, and the unsupported claim must exceed them, such as assuming perfect recognition. Check that the learner distinguishes the two decisions rather than merely naming two devices.

teacher.background: Avoid making AI a yes-or-no property of a whole product before defining the component and decision. Modern learned models and symbolic reasoning both belong in the broader AI discussion. The learning goal here is evidence-based mechanism classification, not memorising a list of smart objects. Do not infer training from responsiveness, language, movement or one correct output.
materials: The bus diagram and photo-library case from the student chapter
Blank paper and three colours of pencil
A copy of workbook tasks W1 to W5; no online accounts or real student data
sessions: Ask the clock prerequisite question. Record observed and inferred statements in separate columns. Read two examples aloud without praising a guess as a fact.
Read the bus case. Trace each row of the diagram with a finger. Ask which decision each row makes. Say that a product can combine mechanisms.
Model the red-display question using claim, relevant evidence and conclusion. Cover the final table row and ask students to justify it.
Pairs complete the photo-library explanation and W1. Listen for a distinction between a predicted label and an album action.
Retrieve the distinction with the speaking-device exit question. Revisit the diagram if students rely on appearance.
Complete W2 and W3 in pairs. Each partner must offer a different possible cause of a misplaced photo or direction change.
Collect W4 as an independent assessment. Do not display its solution or substitute a hinted answer for an independent attempt.
Discuss one anonymised explanation and set W5 as extension or the next opening task. Record which prerequisite needs reteaching.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Prediction stage is learned because labelled examples were used to fit the model; album placement follows the stated written rule; the owner move is human control. Inspect the predicted label and the album action record. A correct answer from a speaking device does not identify the mechanism because recordings, rules, learned models and human messages can all produce speech.
misconceptions: Explain that AI also includes symbolic reasoning. In the specific bus case, the simple colour threshold is automation; the full system contains a fitted predictor.
A correct output proves a learned model
Ask whether a calculator, recording or person could produce the same correct output. Require evidence about fitting or reasoning.
Accept unknown when the learner identifies a specific missing fact and a useful way to obtain it.
teacher.assessment: For W4, require all three components classified with their supplied evidence and an explanation that a downstream rule can operate correctly on a wrong estimate. A label without supporting evidence is developing. If the learner says the display proves accuracy, return to the two bus rows and ask what each row actually checks. After feedback, assess a fresh case rather than awarding independent mastery for the corrected W4 answer.
teacher.support: Read the cases aloud and let students use arrows or spoken explanations. Supply the three mechanism labels if vocabulary is the barrier, but record that support. Extension students should design two mechanisms producing the same output and propose evidence that would distinguish them.
teacher.next: Week 2 follows how information is represented and changed between components. Keep the three-row bus diagram: the delay number and the warning colour are different representations of related information.
